design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of risk differences, written as the evidence base of an American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) practice guideline on the pharmacological management of alcohol withdrawal by the society's working group (chair M. F. Mayo-Smith; JAMA 1997;278:144–151). MEDLINE from 1966 to June 1995, English only; 134 articles with original data, including 65 prospective controlled trials of 42 medications. Meta-analyses only for delirium and seizures: benzodiazepines vs placebo (6 trials, 1961–1983), long- vs short-acting benzodiazepines (3 trials), and phenothiazines vs placebo or cross-tolerant medication (4 trials); other agents and dosing strategies reviewed narratively. Recommendations graded A to C by a published system (Cook et al., 1992). AMSTAR 2 is applied to the meta-analysis, as the round brief directs; the guideline's recommendations are reported only as what it recommended, without regimens or doses. The PDF is a scan; every number on this card was checked on the rendered page.
can_establish: What the 1997 ASAM guideline recommended for the pharmacological management of alcohol withdrawal, and the pooled absolute differences in delirium and seizures between benzodiazepines and placebo, between long- and short-acting benzodiazepines, and between phenothiazines and placebo or cross-tolerant medication, in the trials found up to mid-1995.
cannot_establish: Whether those pooled estimates are unbiased or complete (single-database English-language search, no appraisal of the trials' risk of bias, no heterogeneity or publication-bias analysis, six small placebo-controlled trials from 1961–1983); the effects of particular drugs, doses or regimens; outcomes in people already in delirium or after a seizure (out of scope), or in adolescents, older people, pregnant women or people with comorbid illness (no studies found); or anything published after June 1995.

sample.recruitment: MEDLINE search with the key words substance withdrawal syndrome and ethyl alcohol, from its first entries in 1966 through June 1995, plus references of selected articles and reviews; English-language articles with original clinical data on humans (p. 145, Methods › Review of the Evidence). The pooled trials' settings, participants and recruitment are not described.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies with clinical data; for data extraction and meta-analysis, prospective controlled trials with methodologically sound end points and documented reporting of the end point in question (p. 145). Outside the guideline's scope: patients seen after a withdrawal seizure or with established withdrawal delirium, and the choice of inpatient or outpatient setting; phenytoin had its own earlier guideline (p. 144, Introduction, 3rd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: One database, English only. The six placebo-controlled trials date from 1961 to 1983; the pooled delirium estimate leaves out two of them (Sellers et al. and Naranjo et al., 1983) because they did not report delirium, and the seizure estimate one (Rosenfeld & Bizzoco, 1961). Kaim et al. (1969) supplies 233 of the 358 patients in the delirium analysis and 8 of its 11 placebo-arm cases, and 9 of the 17 placebo-arm seizures (editors' counts from Table 2). No studies were found in adolescents, in older people, in pregnancy or in people with coexisting medical or substance use disorders (p. 148).

exposure.measurement: The interventions as given in the primary trials: benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide in four of the six placebo-controlled trials, diazepam and lorazepam in one each; Table 2), other sedative-hypnotics (chlormethiazole, barbital, tetrabamate, paraldehyde, phenobarbital), β-blockers, clonidine, carbamazepine, neuroleptics (promazine, chlorpromazine), magnesium, ethyl alcohol, thiamine and other agents; and two ways of giving medication, on a fixed schedule or triggered by symptoms measured on a scale.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted. The trials' regimens are not described trial by trial; Table 5 gives example regimens meeting the guideline, which the project does not reproduce (no dosing information). Amounts given in one trial are reported below only as a trial outcome.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the trials. The review names concurrent non-medical sedative-hypnotic use as a risk factor for major complications and advises caution in using withdrawal scales during withdrawal from other drugs (p. 148).

comparison.controls: Placebo (Table 2); other benzodiazepines (Table 3: long-acting chlordiazepoxide or diazepam vs short-acting lorazepam or alprazolam); placebo, or cross-tolerant medication that combines benzodiazepines and paraldehyde (Table 4); fixed-schedule dosing vs symptom-triggered dosing in two randomized trials (text only).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline withdrawal severity, history of seizures or delirium, medical and psychiatric comorbidity and other drug use in the pooled trials are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Seven outcomes: severity of withdrawal and withdrawal delirium, each as defined in DSM-IV; withdrawal seizures; completion of withdrawal; entry into rehabilitation; adverse effects; and cost (acquisition costs from wholesale prices in the 1993 Red Book) (pp. 144–145). Only delirium and seizures were meta-analysed. Withdrawal scales discussed: CIWA-A and its revision, the CIWA-Ar.
outcomes.validity_norms: The pooled trials (1961–1986) predate DSM-IV (1994); how their definitions of delirium and seizures were matched to DSM-IV is not described.
outcomes.operationalization: Delirium and seizures as numbers of patients with the event in each arm; withdrawal severity by a count of trials favouring each drug (no pooled estimate).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two-tailed tests with significance at P≤.05 (p. 145). The 7 counted here are the pooled estimates (2 in Table 2, 1 in Table 3, 4 in Table 4); 7 outcomes were also listed, of which 2 were pooled.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the trials; not applicable at review level.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects meta-analysis of risk differences (refs 13–15); single-trial comparisons by Fisher exact test with Taylor-series 95% CIs for relative risks. Benzodiazepine vs placebo: delirium −4.9 cases per 100 patients (95% CI −9.0 to −0.7), P=.04, 4 trials; seizures −7.7 per 100 (−12.0 to −3.5), P<.001 in Table 2 and P=.003 in the abstract and text, 5 trials. Long- vs short-acting benzodiazepines, seizures: −6.7 per 100 (−13.0 to −0.0), P=.07, 3 trials. Phenothiazine vs placebo: delirium 0.0 per 100 (−5.8 to +6.6), P=.92; seizures +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9), P=.19. Phenothiazine vs cross-tolerant medication: delirium +6.6 (+2.4 to +10.8), P=.002; seizures +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6), P<.001. Kaim et al. (1969) alone: chlordiazepoxide vs placebo, delirium RR 0.16 (0.02–1.24), P=.08, seizures RR 0.14 (0.02–1.09), P=.046; chlorpromazine vs chlordiazepoxide, delirium RR 7.4 (0.9–54), P=.03, seizures RR 12.6 (1.6–95), P=.001. Editors' sums from Table 2: delirium 3/172 (1.7%) with benzodiazepines vs 11/186 (5.9%) with placebo; seizures 1/182 (0.5%) vs 17/196 (8.7%); editors' calculation from the pooled risk differences: about 20 patients treated per delirium case avoided and about 13 per seizure avoided. Symptom-triggered vs fixed-schedule dosing (two randomized trials): significantly less medication and shorter treatment (abstract, P<.001); in the larger trial, median chlordiazepoxide 100 mg vs 425 mg and median duration 9 vs 68 hours, reported as trial outcomes.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned. The draft guideline was reviewed by first authors of included articles from the past 10 years and representatives of 68 medical organizations; the ASAM board of directors approved it in June 1996, with review and revision scheduled for June 2001 (p. 145).
analysis.selective_reporting: Delirium was not reported in two of the six placebo-controlled trials and seizures in one; withdrawal severity, completion of withdrawal, entry into rehabilitation and adverse effects are described without pooled estimates; heterogeneity is never reported; the effectiveness outcomes of the two trials of symptom-triggered dosing are not given; the minimally clinically significant benefit on which the grades depend is not stated.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The review says the trials of several agents (chlormethiazole, barbital, tetrabamate, β-blockers, clonidine, magnesium) were too small to judge effects on delirium or seizures. Event counts in the benzodiazepine–placebo analyses are low: 3 vs 11 delirium cases and 1 vs 17 seizures (editors' sums).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six small placebo-controlled trials from 1961–1983 (four of chlordiazepoxide), benzodiazepines were associated with 4.9 fewer cases of delirium per 100 patients (95% CI 0.7 to 9.0 fewer; 3 vs 11 events) and 7.7 fewer seizures per 100 (3.5 to 12.0 fewer; 1 vs 17 events). In three trials, long-acting agents had 6.7 fewer seizures per 100 than short-acting ones (P=.07). Phenothiazines did not differ from placebo in delirium or seizures but had more of both than benzodiazepines or paraldehyde. Two randomized trials found symptom-triggered dosing used less medication and shorter treatment than fixed schedules. For other agents, trials showed relief of symptoms but were too small for delirium or seizures, and no studies were found in adolescents, older people, pregnancy or comorbid illness.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and recommendations match most of this, with these gaps. (1) The text says neuroleptics “increase the incidence of seizures compared with placebo” (p. 147), and the grade A recommendation against neuroleptic monotherapy gives increased seizures as a reason (p. 149), while the pooled comparison with placebo is +4.6 per 100 (−2.6 to +11.9; P=.19); more seizures are shown only against benzodiazepines or paraldehyde. (2) The recommendations state “There is no evidence that the recommendations should change” for adolescents or older people (p. 149), after a results section that found no studies in adolescents and none of treatment approaches in older people (p. 148): an absence of studies is presented as an absence of difference. (3) The abstract says benzodiazepines reduce withdrawal severity; this rests on a count of six trials without a pooled estimate, and one of the six cited references is an evaluation of a social-setting detoxification programme (p. 145). (4) The grades depend on a minimally clinically significant benefit that is never stated, and level I labels are given to findings resting on one cited trial of 40 patients (a smoother withdrawal with long-acting agents) or partly on reviews (potential for non-medical use). (5) The grade A recommendation for individualized, scale-guided dosing rests on two randomized trials, the larger co-authored by the guideline's author, whose effectiveness results are summarized only as equivalent. The core conclusion, that benzodiazepines are suitable agents with fewer seizures and delirium than placebo, is in line with the pooled data.

timeline.event: The six placebo-controlled trials pooled in Table 2 span 1961 to 1983 (Rosenfeld & Bizzoco, 1961; Sereny & Kalant, 1965; Kaim et al., 1969; Zilm et al., 1980; Sellers et al., 1983; Naranjo et al., 1983).
Sullivan et al., the revised CIWA-Ar scale (ref 157; first author a working-group member; on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B); not read here.

Saitz et al., randomized double-blind trial of symptom-triggered vs fixed-schedule treatment (ref 146; co-authored by M. F. Mayo-Smith; on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B), the larger trial behind the grade A recommendation for individualized dosing; not read here.
Kasser et al., ASAM guideline on phenytoin in alcohol withdrawal (ref 9), written by members of the same working group.
ASAM board of directors approved this guideline in June 1996, with review and revision scheduled for June 2001 (p. 145).

Mayo-Smith et al., ASAM evidence-based guideline on the management of alcohol withdrawal delirium (on the project's Alcohol list, Tier B), the topic this paper left to a separate guideline; not read here.

Amato et al., Cochrane review of benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal (on the project's Alcohol list; card being written by another reader in this round), and Minozzi et al., Cochrane review of anticonvulsants for alcohol withdrawal (Tier B; not read here).
Schuckit, review of the recognition and management of withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens); not read here.
ASAM guideline on alcohol withdrawal management, named among the known gaps of the project's Alcohol list; not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The guideline's central pooled result (fewer seizures and delirium with benzodiazepines than placebo) rests on six small trials from 1961–1983 found by a 1995 MEDLINE search; later syntheses on the project list (Amato et al., 2010) should be preferred for current effect estimates once read. This paper is cited for what the 1997 ASAM guideline recommended and for its pooled estimates as reported, labelled as from a review rated critically low in confidence. Its secondary claims (long- vs short-acting agents, P=.07; neuroleptic seizure risk against placebo, not significant; special populations, no studies) were not settled by it. No correction notice is on file or mentioned in the PDF; none was searched for in this reading.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement. The guideline was produced for the ASAM Committee on Practice Guidelines; reprint requests to the California Society of Addiction Medicine (p. 144, first-page footnotes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Working group (p. 149): M. F. Mayo-Smith (chair; Ambulatory Care Service, Veterans Affairs Medical Center, Manchester, NH, and Harvard Medical School), P. Cushman Jr, A. J. Hill, G. Jara (California Society of Addiction Medicine), C. Kasser, M. Kraus, D. Nauts, R. Saitz, J. W. Smith, J. T. Sullivan (Department of Clinical Pharmacology, Bayer Corporation, West Haven, Conn) and N. Thiessen. Several cited primary studies have authors whose names match working-group members: Saitz and Mayo-Smith (the 1994 symptom-triggered trial, ref 146, and a 1995 national practice survey, ref 6), Sullivan (CIWA-Ar, ref 157; ref 132), Kraus (atenolol trials, refs 86 and 115), Cushman (adrenergic-agonist and lofexidine studies, refs 82, 83 and 111), Kasser, Smith, Thiessen and Mayo-Smith (the phenytoin guideline, ref 9), and Mayo-Smith (late-onset seizures, ref 149). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A current, registered systematic review with several databases and no language limit, per-trial risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity and small-study analyses; and adequately powered randomized trials comparing benzodiazepine strategies (symptom-triggered vs fixed schedule; long- vs short-acting agents) on seizures and delirium, including older people, pregnant women and people with medical comorbidity, for whom this review found no studies.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people in alcohol withdrawal), interventions (any pharmacological agent) and seven outcomes are stated; comparators are not specified and appear only in the tables.
No protocol or a priori plan is mentioned; the review predates review registries, so this reflects the standards of its time rather than a judgment of intent.

All studies with original clinical data were reviewed and prospective controlled trials pooled, with a design hierarchy used for grading (Table 1), but no reason is given for the designs included or for pooling only prospective controlled trials.

MEDLINE only (1966 to June 1995) with one pair of key words, English only without justification, plus reference lists of selected articles and reviews; no second database, trial registry or grey literature. Partial yes needs at least two databases.
Not reported; only data extraction is said to be duplicated.
Two reviewers independently extracted data from each prospective controlled trial with sound end points (p. 145, Methods › Review of the Evidence).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies; trials were kept only if their end points were methodologically sound and documented, without saying which failed and why.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2–4 give first author, year, agents and event counts per arm only; populations, settings, severity, regimens, follow-up and whether each trial was randomized or blinded are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No trial-level assessment of randomization, allocation concealment, blinding or attrition. Table 1's levels classify designs and error rates for grading recommendations, and the paper does not say which trials were rated level I or II.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of risk differences (refs 13–15) lets trials with zero events contribute, but different drugs (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, lorazepam) and comparators (benzodiazepines and paraldehyde as cross-tolerant medication) are combined without stated justification, randomized and non-randomized controlled trials are not distinguished, and heterogeneity is neither reported nor investigated.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of how trial quality affects the pooled estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The introduction says the trials generally involved few subjects and were of uncertain quality, and the results flag small trials for several agents, but the pooled benzodiazepine and neuroleptic results and their grades are interpreted without regard to the trials' risk of bias.
No heterogeneity statistic or discussion for any pooled estimate.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement for the review; one working-group member is affiliated with Bayer Corporation, and several members wrote cited primary studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Seven critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15), which gives critically low confidence. This measures the review against current standards, several of which (protocol registries, trial-level risk-of-bias tools) were not usual in 1995–1997; it is not a judgment of the guideline's clinical value. Consequences: the pooled benzodiazepine estimates rest on six small trials from 1961–1983, found by a single-database English-language search and not appraised for bias; the delirium estimate rests on 3 vs 11 events; heterogeneity and publication bias are unknown; and the grade A labels depend on an unstated threshold of clinically significant benefit. Citable for what the 1997 ASAM guideline recommended, graded as it graded them, and for its pooled estimates as reported, with this rating; current claims about benzodiazepines for withdrawal should rest on later systematic reviews (Amato et al., 2010, on the project list) once read.

key_findings.finding: Methods: MEDLINE searched with the key words substance withdrawal syndrome and ethyl alcohol from 1966 through June 1995 (abstract: English-language articles published before 1 July 1995), plus references of selected articles and reviews; articles with original clinical data on humans underwent structured review; prospective controlled trials with methodologically sound end points were extracted by 2 reviewers independently; single-trial differences tested by the Fisher exact test with Taylor-series 95% CIs for relative risks; meta-analysis, when appropriate, by a random-effects model with risk differences; two-tailed tests, significance at P≤.05.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Data Sources, Study Selection, Data Abstraction), p. 144; Methods › Review of the Evidence, p. 145

key_findings.finding: Scope and outcomes: seven outcomes (withdrawal severity and withdrawal delirium as defined in DSM-IV, seizures, completion of withdrawal, entry into rehabilitation, adverse effects, cost); not addressed: patients seen after a withdrawal seizure or with established delirium, and the choice of inpatient or outpatient setting, left to separate guidelines; phenytoin covered by an earlier ASAM guideline. The introduction says alcohol dependence occurs in 15% to 20% of primary care and hospitalized patients and that withdrawal trials generally involved few subjects and were often of uncertain quality.

Pooled risk difference −4.9 cases of delirium per 100 patients (95% CI −9.0 to −0.7), P=.04.

Kaim et al. contribute 233 of the 358 patients and 8 of the 11 placebo-arm cases (editors' count).

Pooled risk difference −7.7 seizures per 100 patients (95% CI −12.0 to −3.5), P<.001 in Table 2.

Editors' sums from Table 2: 1/182 (0.5%) vs 17/196 (8.7%); editors' calculation from the pooled difference: about 13 patients treated per seizure avoided. The Cochrane review (Amato et al., 2010; sc_amato_2010) gives Naranjo et al. (1983) as 0 of 21 against 1 of 20, not 0 of 15 against 2 of 15; neither review explains the difference.

key_findings.finding: Signs and symptoms: six prospective trials involving 5 agents all found benzodiazepines more effective than placebo in reducing the signs and symptoms of withdrawal, and trials comparing benzodiazepines found all similarly effective; no pooled estimate of withdrawal severity is given.

key_findings.finding: Long- vs short-acting benzodiazepines, seizures (Table 3): Solomon et al. 1983, chlordiazepoxide 0/25 vs lorazepam 2/25; Wilson & Vulcano 1984, chlordiazepoxide 5/50 vs alprazolam 9/50; Ritson & Chick 1986, diazepam 0/20 vs lorazepam 1/20. Pooled risk difference with long-acting agents −6.7 seizures per 100 (95% CI −13.0 to −0.0), P=.07, which the text calls a trend. Longer-acting agents are said to give a smoother withdrawal with less breakthrough or rebound (one cited trial) and, on pharmacological data and clinical experience, to risk excess sedation in older people and people with marked liver disease; there are few data on delirium.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 146); Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 145)
key_findings.note: Editors' sums: 5/95 with long-acting vs 12/95 with short-acting agents. The printed interval and P value disagree (reporting issue 4).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; Table 3 read on the page rendered at 600 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Potential for non-medical use: the trials and reviews cited (refs 65, 151–153) show that some benzodiazepines are preferred by people with addictive disorders; agents of rapid onset (diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam) have higher potential than slower-onset agents (chlordiazepoxide, oxazepam, halazepam), which the review says may matter in outpatient settings or for people with a history of benzodiazepine or other substance use problems, while faster onset may help when rapid control of symptoms is needed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Costs: published case reports of continuous infusions of short-acting benzodiazepines give drug costs of $50 335 for a 25-hour midazolam infusion in one patient and $26 045 for another patient's stay; no evidence was found that infusions give better outcomes than oral or intravenous bolus treatment with longer-acting agents; in one institution, a guideline favouring longer-acting agents over infusions was followed by a fall in mean costs from $1008.72 to $59.79 per patient, with equivalent outcomes and no more adverse effects.
key_findings.locator: Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The text spells midazolam as midalozam. The same paragraph lists 1993 wholesale prices per tablet at roughly equivalent doses; not extracted because they are tied to doses.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Other sedative-hypnotics: chlormethiazole was better than placebo, and barbital and tetrabamate equal to benzodiazepines, for signs and symptoms, in trials too small to judge seizures or delirium; paraldehyde has only case series and one trial (superior to promazine); barbiturates are used by about 10% of US detoxification programmes, but no controlled trial of phenobarbital was found, only uncontrolled studies in support; phenobarbital is described as long acting, inexpensive and of low potential for non-medical use, and barbiturates, phenobarbital included, as carrying a greater risk of respiratory depression, particularly with alcohol, and a lower safety margin than benzodiazepines at high doses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal scales: the CIWA-A and its shortened revision, the CIWA-Ar, are described as reliable, reproducible and valid against ratings by experienced clinicians, usable in detoxification and psychiatric units and by nursing staff on general medical and surgical wards; high scores predict seizures and delirium.
key_findings.locator: Results › Structured Assessment Scales and Determination of Dosage, 1st paragraph
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Symptom-triggered dosing: many patients go through withdrawal with only minor symptoms despite little or no medication; in two randomized trials, giving medication only when a structured scale crosses a severity threshold was as effective as fixed-schedule dosing, with significantly less medication and a significantly shorter treatment; in the larger trial (Saitz et al., 1994), median chlordiazepoxide was 100 mg vs 425 mg and median duration of treatment 9 vs 68 hours. Seizures were not observed in series treated with symptom-triggered therapy.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Data Synthesis (p. 144); Results › Structured Assessment Scales and Determination of Dosage, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 146)
key_findings.note: Amounts are trial outcomes, not doses to use. The abstract gives P<.001 for less medication and shorter treatment; the text gives no P value and no effectiveness results (reporting issue 6). M. F. Mayo-Smith is a co-author of the larger trial (ref 146).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on pages rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: β-Blockers: some evidence that they reduce manifestations of withdrawal, mainly autonomic ones; they have no known anticonvulsant activity and no study was large enough to show whether they reduce or increase seizures; delirium is a known side effect of β-blockers that enter the brain well, such as propranolol, and was increased with propranolol in at least one study; they may mask other withdrawal signs and hinder scale-guided treatment (a case report of delayed recognition of delirium).
key_findings.locator: Results › β-Adrenergic Antagonists (begins p. 146, continued p. 147)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; read on pages rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Clonidine: well-designed studies consistently show symptom relief in mild to moderate withdrawal, with no study large enough for delirium or seizures. Carbamazepine: superior to placebo and equal to barbital and oxazepam in mild to moderate withdrawal, with limited data on seizures or delirium; without significant haematological or hepatic toxicity in 7-day protocols; associated with less psychiatric distress and a faster return to work; prevents withdrawal seizures in animal studies; described as not adding to alcohol's central nervous system and respiratory depression and as having no potential for non-medical use.

key_findings.finding: Neuroleptics (Table 4): Thomas & Freedman 1964, promazine 4/34 vs paraldehyde 0/33 delirium; Sereny & Kalant 1965, promazine 1/23, placebo 1/11, chlordiazepoxide 0/24 delirium and 2/23, 0/11, 0/24 seizures; Chambers & Schultz 1965, promazine 5/34, diazepam 0/35, chlordiazepoxide 0/34 seizures; Kaim et al. 1969, chlorpromazine 7/98, placebo 8/130, chlordiazepoxide 1/103 delirium and 12/98, 9/130, 1/103 seizures. Pooled risk differences, phenothiazine vs placebo: delirium 0.0 per 100 (95% CI −5.8 to +6.6), P=.92; seizures +4.6 per 100 (−2.6 to +11.9), P=.19. Phenothiazine vs cross-tolerant medication (benzodiazepine or paraldehyde): delirium +6.6 per 100 (+2.4 to +10.8), P=.002; seizures +11.4 per 100 (+6.2 to +16.6), P<.001. The agents studied, chlorpromazine and promazine, are said to be among those with the greatest effect on seizure threshold; uncontrolled experience supports neuroleptics for calming agitation.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Neuroleptic Agents
key_findings.note: The text gives 12.4 for the seizure difference against benzodiazepines (Table 4: 11.4) and says these agents increase seizures compared with placebo, which the pooled comparison with placebo does not show (reporting issues 2 and 3).

key_findings.finding: Magnesium: levels are usually normal on admission, fall during withdrawal and recover as symptoms subside; one double-blind placebo-controlled trial of intramuscular magnesium added to benzodiazepines found no difference in withdrawal severity, seizures or delirium, with limited power for the latter two. Ethyl alcohol: only small uncontrolled case series without objective severity measures, and no controlled trials against placebo or benzodiazepines; intravenous infusion needs close monitoring and has toxicity and infusion-site risks. Thiamine: in one large trial it did not reduce delirium or seizures, but thiamine deficiency is frequent in people with alcohol dependence and its administration prevents Wernicke disease and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Other agents: some relieve withdrawal, none has been shown to reduce delirium or seizures.

key_findings.finding: Special populations: no studies were identified on withdrawal management in adolescents, on treatment approaches in older people, in pregnant women, or in people with specific coexisting medical or substance use disorders. Ethyl alcohol is called a well-known teratogen; retrospective studies associate benzodiazepines and barbiturates with congenital malformation, and a recent study associated in-utero phenobarbital exposure with intelligence deficits; the review judges these risks small against the harm to the fetus of severe withdrawal or seizures. Concurrent non-medical sedative-hypnotic use is a risk factor for major complications; one cohort of psychiatric inpatients found symptom-triggered treatment with a long-acting benzodiazepine safe and effective.

key_findings.finding: Grading (Table 1, from Cook et al., 1992): evidence levels from I (randomized trials with low false-positive and low false-negative errors) to V (case series without controls); grade A = at least one level I study, or a meta-analysis whose confidence limit exceeds the minimally clinically significant benefit; grade B = at least one level II study, or a meta-analysis whose estimate but not its confidence limit exceeds that benefit; grade C = data other than prospective controlled trials. Greatest value was placed on patient safety, then on facilitating treatment of alcohol dependence, patient comfort and cost. The draft was reviewed by first authors of included articles from the past 10 years and by representatives of 68 medical organizations; the ASAM board approved it in June 1996, with review due in June 2001.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Methods › Recommendations; Methods › Guideline Review
key_findings.note: The minimally clinically significant benefit is never quantified, and the paper does not say which trials were rated level I or II (reporting issue 9).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf (scanned; Table 1 read on the page rendered at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Recommendation, choice of agent: benzodiazepines are recommended as suitable agents for alcohol withdrawal (grade A); all appear equally effective for signs and symptoms, and the choice among them can be guided by five considerations: long-acting agents may prevent seizures better (level II evidence) and give a smoother withdrawal with fewer rebound symptoms (level I); short-acting agents may carry less risk of oversedation (level III); some benzodiazepines have a higher potential for non-medical use (level I); costs vary considerably. Benzodiazepines are recommended over most other sedative-hypnotics; phenobarbital is a clinically acceptable alternative with a possibly lower safety margin when high doses are needed (grade C).
key_findings.locator: Recommendations › Choice of Pharmacological Agent, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Recommendation, approach to dosing (reported without regimens or doses): treatment should be individualized so that patients can receive large amounts of medication rapidly if needed (grade A); in specialist addiction treatment programmes, structured scales such as the CIWA-Ar are recommended for initial assessment and monitoring (grade A), with caution in concurrent medical or psychiatric illness or withdrawal from other drugs. By scale-rated severity: in mild withdrawal, supportive non-drug care with monitoring is a reasonable option (level I); moderate withdrawal benefits from medication, which also lowers the risk of major complications; severe withdrawal carries a significant risk of major complications if untreated (level I), and benzodiazepines are recommended in the amounts needed to control symptoms, with close monitoring. With a history of withdrawal seizures, giving medication at presentation regardless of severity is a reasonable option (level III), as is symptom-triggered treatment alone; with notable medical comorbidity, medication should be considered even in mild to moderate withdrawal; people using sedative-hypnotics may be at higher risk and show tolerance (level III). Where staff are not trained in scale-guided treatment, fixed-schedule treatment with additional medication when needed is an acceptable alternative, trading possibly unnecessary medication for a margin of safety. Table 5 gives example regimens (not extracted).

key_findings.finding: Recommendation, other agents: β-blockers, clonidine and carbamazepine are not recommended as monotherapy (grade B) but may be used with benzodiazepines in particular coexisting conditions (coronary artery disease for β-blockers, opiate withdrawal for clonidine, benzodiazepine withdrawal for carbamazepine); neuroleptics should not be used as monotherapy because they do not reduce delirium and increase seizures (grade A), but may be added to benzodiazepines for marked agitation or hallucinations; routine parenteral magnesium is not recommended (grade B); ethyl alcohol is not recommended (grade C); thiamine should be given to all patients with alcohol dependence at initial examination (grade C).

key_findings.finding: Recommendation, special populations: “There is no evidence that the recommendations should change” for adolescents or older people; the possibly lower oversedation risk of shorter-acting benzodiazepines may matter in older people (grade C); ethyl alcohol should not be used in pregnant women (grade C); in pregnancy, benzodiazepines and barbiturates should be limited to the amount needed to prevent the major complications of withdrawal (grade C).

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled seizure risk difference for benzodiazepines vs placebo (−7.7 per 100, 95% CI −12.0 to −3.5) has P<.001 in Table 2 but P=.003 in the abstract and the Results text.
reporting_issues.page: p. 144 (Abstract, Data Synthesis); p. 145 (Table 2; Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Both values indicate a clear difference; claims should cite the estimate with its interval rather than either P value.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the excess of seizures with phenothiazines over benzodiazepines as 12.4 per 100 (P<.001), where Table 4 gives +11.4 (95% CI +6.2 to +16.6) for phenothiazine vs cross-tolerant medication.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the table value; an editors' recalculation from the Table 4 counts (DerSimonian–Laird random effects on risk differences, 0.5 added to zero cells for the variance) gives about +11.5 per 100, consistent with the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says neuroleptics “increase the incidence of seizures compared with placebo”, and the grade A recommendation against neuroleptic monotherapy gives increased seizures as a reason, but Table 4's pooled comparison with placebo is +4.6 per 100 (95% CI −2.6 to +11.9), P=.19.
reporting_issues.page: p. 147 (Results › Neuroleptic Agents; Table 4); p. 149 (Recommendations › Other Agents)
reporting_issues.consequence: More seizures are shown only against benzodiazepines or paraldehyde; a claim that neuroleptics increase seizures relative to no active drug is not supported by these data.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3's pooled seizure difference for long- vs short-acting benzodiazepines is printed as −6.7 per 100 with a 95% CI of −13.0 to −0.0 but P=.07; an interval ending at zero implies P of about .05.
reporting_issues.consequence: An editors' recalculation from the Table 3 counts (method as in issue 2) gives about −7.0 per 100 (−14.4 to +0.5), P=.07, an interval that includes zero; the long-acting advantage for seizures is not statistically established, as the text's word trend implies.

reporting_issues.issue: For Kaim et al. (1969), the Taylor-series interval includes 1 while the Fisher exact P is below .05 for chlordiazepoxide vs placebo on seizures (RR 0.14, 0.02–1.09, P=.046) and for chlorpromazine vs chlordiazepoxide on delirium (RR 7.4, 0.9–54, P=.03).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two methods give different verdicts. An editors' recalculation reproduces the printed P values (.08, .046, .03, .001) and intervals, except the upper limit of the chlorpromazine delirium interval (about 59 rather than 54); none of this changes the pooled results.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's P<.001 for less medication and shorter treatment with scale-guided dosing does not appear in the text or a table, and the effectiveness results of the two trials are summarized only as equivalent.
reporting_issues.page: p. 144 (Abstract, Data Synthesis); p. 146 (Results › Structured Assessment Scales and Determination of Dosage, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The P value cannot be traced within the paper; claims should cite the trials (Saitz et al., 1994; Manikant et al., 1993) for effect sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 dates Wilson and Vulcano (ref 90) 1984; the reference list dates it 1985.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the year from the reference list.

reporting_issues.issue: Several citation numbers do not match the topic of the reference they point to, judged by its title: ref 61 (an evaluation of a social-setting detoxification programme) among the six trials showing benzodiazepines better than placebo; ref 88 (a halazepam trial) among β-blocker studies; ref 52 (a report on injectable lorazepam) among clonidine studies; ref 82 (adrenergic-agonist therapy) among carbamazepine studies; ref 80 (the magnesium trial) among case series of ethyl alcohol.
reporting_issues.page: p. 145 (Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 1st paragraph); pp. 146–147 (β-Adrenergic Antagonists; Clonidine footnote; Carbamazepine; Ethyl Alcohol); references pp. 149–151
reporting_issues.consequence: Some statements cannot be traced to their evidence, and the count of six placebo-controlled trials behind the claim that benzodiazepines reduce withdrawal severity may include a study that is not one.

reporting_issues.issue: The grades depend on a minimally clinically significant benefit that is never quantified, and the paper does not say which trials it rated level I or II.
reporting_issues.consequence: The A and B grades cannot be checked against the pooled intervals; whether the delirium result (interval reaching −0.7 per 100) meets grade A depends on a threshold the paper does not give.

reporting_issues.issue: Level I evidence is assigned to a smoother withdrawal with long-acting agents, which rests on one cited trial (ref 98) with 20 patients per arm in Table 3, and to the higher potential of some benzodiazepines for non-medical use, whose citations include a book-chapter review and a task-force report as well as trials.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 145–146 (Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; Table 3); p. 148 (Recommendations › Choice of Pharmacological Agent)
reporting_issues.consequence: The level labels overstate the evidence where it is one small trial or a review; claims should cite the underlying studies and their size.

reporting_issues.issue: Outcomes are said to correspond to DSM-IV definitions, but the pooled trials date from 1961 to 1986, before DSM-IV (1994), and how their definitions of delirium and seizures were matched is not described.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 144–145 (Abstract, Data Abstraction; Methods › Outcomes); Tables 2–4
reporting_issues.consequence: Outcome definitions may differ across the pooled trials; a pooled risk difference for delirium combines whatever each trial counted.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled risk differences for benzodiazepines against placebo in Table 2 (delirium −4.9 per 100, 95% CI −9.0 to −0.7; seizures −7.7, −12.0 to −3.5) are reproduced exactly by DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling of risk differences without any continuity correction (editors' recalculation from the Table 2 counts). Under that method the trials with no events in either arm (Zilm et al., 1980, for delirium; Sereny and Kalant, 1965, for seizures) drop out, so the estimates rest on 3 and 4 trials, and arms with no events contribute no variance. With 0.5 added to zero cells for the variance, the estimates are −4.3 (−8.2 to −0.3) and −6.7 (−10.7 to −2.6).
reporting_issues.page: p. 145 (Table 2; Methods › Review of the Evidence)
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction and significance hold under the more conservative calculation; the printed intervals are somewhat narrower than they would be with zero cells handled conventionally, and the pooled delirium estimate rests on three trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled phenothiazine-against-placebo estimates in Table 4 are not reproduced from the trial counts: the delirium estimate is printed as 0.0 per 100 although its own interval (−5.8 to +6.6) is centred on about +0.4, which a recalculation gives (+0.4, −5.8 to +6.6); the seizure estimate, printed as +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9), recalculates to +6.4 (−0.1 to +12.9) without a continuity correction and +5.9 (−1.1 to +13.0) with one (editors' recalculation, DerSimonian–Laird).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: every method gives intervals that include no difference against placebo, so reporting issue 2 (no shown increase in seizures against placebo) stands; the printed point estimates should not be quoted as exact.
